practice.context: A documentary page says, “Mangroves reduce wave energy,” while a diagram shows roots slowing arrows labelled “water movement”. What comprehension move best connects the modes?
practice.correct: Link the written claim with the diagram’s arrows to build a clearer explanation of how mangroves reduce wave energy.
distractors: Treat the diagram and sentence as unrelated.
Use the diagram only because pictures are always more reliable.
Ignore the words once a visual is present.
practice.rationale: Comprehension improves when readers connect information across print and images rather than treating each mode separately.
practice.hint: Ask what each mode adds to the same idea.

practice.context: In a text about pollination, the words “pollen”, “stigma” and “nectar” appear repeatedly. What should a reader do with this topic vocabulary?
practice.correct: Clarify the meanings and use them to build a more precise understanding of the process.
distractors: Replace all technical terms with “stuff”.
Skip every unfamiliar word.
Memorise spellings without connecting them to meaning.
practice.rationale: Topic-specific vocabulary carries important concepts needed to understand specialised information.
practice.hint: Identify and clarify words that are central to the topic.

practice.context: A paragraph explains that city trees cool streets by providing shade and releasing water vapour. Which statement is the main idea?
practice.correct: City trees can lower street temperatures in more than one way.
distractors: Water vapour is invisible.
Some streets have traffic.
Shade can occur at lunchtime.
practice.rationale: A main idea captures the central point supported by the paragraph’s details.
practice.hint: Combine the supporting details into the broader point they explain.

practice.context: An article argues that the school should install bottle-refill stations. It says students use many disposable bottles, but gives no source or count. How should a reader evaluate the evidence?
practice.correct: The claim may be reasonable, but the evidence is weak until a reliable source or specific data supports it.
distractors: The argument is proven because it sounds sensible.
No evidence is needed for school decisions.
The claim must be false because no number is supplied.
practice.rationale: Readers evaluate whether evidence is relevant, sufficient and supported by reliable sources.
practice.hint: Separate the claim from the quality of the evidence offered for it.

practice.context: A reader finishes a paragraph but realises they cannot explain what “evaporation” means in the passage. What is the best monitoring strategy?
practice.correct: Pause, re-read the relevant sentence, check the context or glossary, then continue when the meaning is clear.
distractors: Continue reading faster.
Guess and never check.
Restart the whole book even if only one term is unclear.
practice.rationale: Self-monitoring means noticing a breakdown in understanding and choosing a targeted strategy to repair it.
practice.hint: Notice confusion early and choose the smallest useful repair strategy.

practice.context: A teacher-selected text by a First Nations Australian illustrator uses repeated shapes and colours, and the accompanying source notes explain what those choices mean in that particular work. What is the most responsible interpretation?
practice.correct: Use the source notes to discuss how the repeated visual choices contribute to meaning in this specific work, without assuming they mean the same thing across all First Nations cultures.
distractors: Assume every similar colour has one universal Indigenous meaning.
Ignore the illustrator’s context and invent a symbolic meaning.
Treat the visual pattern as decoration only because it is not written text.
practice.rationale: Culturally responsive comprehension uses source-specific evidence and avoids generalising one creator’s choices to all Peoples, Countries or Places.
practice.hint: Ground interpretation in the named creator, text and source context.

test.context: A news page includes a graph showing rainfall totals and a paragraph explaining that the wettest month was March. What is the best way to combine the information?
test.correct: Use the graph to verify and compare rainfall amounts while the paragraph states the key conclusion.
distractors: Choose only the paragraph because graphs are optional.
Choose only the graph because words are biased.
Assume both modes must contain identical information.
test.rationale: Readers build meaning by connecting complementary information across modes.
test.hint: Compare what each mode contributes to the same topic.

test.context: A paragraph states that a wetland supports frogs, insects and waterbirds, then gives one sentence about each. What is the main idea?
test.correct: The wetland provides habitat for several kinds of animals.
distractors: Frogs can jump.
Insects are small.
Waterbirds have feathers.
test.rationale: The main idea is the broader point supported by the details about several animal groups.
test.hint: Ask what all the supporting details are helping to show.

test.context: A persuasive article cites a council water report with measured household use, then claims shorter showers could reduce consumption. Why is this stronger than an unsupported claim?
test.correct: The argument connects its recommendation to relevant evidence from an identifiable source.
distractors: Any government source makes every conclusion automatically true.
Numbers are persuasive even when unrelated.
Recommendations do not need reasoning if a report is mentioned.
test.rationale: Strong arguments use relevant evidence and reasoning, while readers still consider source quality and whether the evidence supports the claim.
test.hint: Check source, relevance and the reasoning link between evidence and claim.

test.context: While reading, a student predicts that a character will miss the bus, but the next paragraph says the bus is delayed. What should the student do?
test.correct: Revise the prediction using the new evidence and continue monitoring whether it still fits.
distractors: Keep the original prediction no matter what.
Ignore the new paragraph.
Change the prediction randomly.
test.rationale: Predictions are provisional and should be updated when new textual evidence changes what is likely.
test.hint: Use new evidence to confirm, refine or reject a prediction.
